### phagocytosis (GO:0006909) 

Phagocytosis is a specialized vesicle-mediated process through which professional phagocytes engulf extracellular particulate material, enclose it within membrane-bound phagosomes, and subsequently fuse these compartments with lysosomes to degrade and recycle the ingested cargo. In the nervous system, this pathway is executed primarily by microglia, although astrocytes can also acquire phagocytic properties under pathological conditions. Phagocytosis is not limited to host defense against microbes; it is also essential for tissue homeostasis through the clearance of apoptotic cells, protein aggregates, damaged myelin, synaptic material, and other cellular debris. The process depends on sequential recognition of targets through surface receptors, cytoskeletal remodeling required for engulfment, phagosome formation, and phagolysosomal maturation for cargo digestion. Multiple receptor systems regulate these steps, including scavenger receptors, purinergic receptors, and the TYRO3, AXL, and MER proto-oncogene, tyrosine kinase family, which often mediate non-inflammatory clearance of phosphatidylserine-exposing material. In the brain, phagocytosis has a dual biological role: when appropriately regulated, it limits inflammation and promotes repair by removing toxic aggregates and debris; when impaired, harmful material accumulates and sustains inflammatory stress; when excessive or misdirected, viable neurons, synapses, or myelin may be inappropriately removed, thereby contributing to neurodegeneration. Thus, phagocytosis is best understood as a tightly regulated homeostatic and immunological pathway whose functional consequences depend on cell type, receptor context, metabolic state, and disease stage.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that phagocytosis is closely linked to Parkinson disease through microglial handling of alpha-synuclein aggregates, myelin debris, inflammatory tone, and Parkin-related regulation of engulfment machinery. The most direct evidence comes from the demonstration that MER proto-oncogene, tyrosine kinase mediates uptake of alpha-synuclein fibrils by human microglia; pharmacological inhibition or gene silencing reduced fibril internalization, whereas this pathway appeared non-inflammatory and may therefore help limit aggregate spread in synucleinopathies, including Parkinson disease (PubMed:37671615). Complementing this observation, inhibition of cluster of differentiation twenty-two restored microglial clearance of alpha-synuclein fibrils in vivo, indicating that anti-phagocytic checkpoints can restrain aggregate removal and that relieving such inhibition may re-establish protective homeostatic phagocytosis in the ageing brain, a major context for Parkinson disease vulnerability (PubMed:30944478). Human single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis across dementia subtypes further identified a distinct microglial state in Parkinson disease dementia characterized by increased macrophage scavenger receptor one expression and enhanced myelin phagocytosis, together with evidence of microglia-oligodendrocyte interaction, suggesting that phagocytosis in Parkinson-related dementia may extend beyond protein aggregate clearance to include responses to myelin injury and white matter remodeling (PubMed:40826098). More broadly, review and experimental studies support the view that microglial phagocytosis can be either protective or harmful in neurodegeneration: efficient clearance of debris and aggregates may promote resolution and repair, whereas excessive engulfment of stressed but viable neurons or synapses may amplify tissue loss (PubMed:33608912; PubMed:32582172). This duality appears particularly relevant to Parkinson disease, in which chronic microglial activation, neuronal stress signals, and extracellular alpha-synuclein may shift phagocytosis from beneficial clearance toward maladaptive pruning. A particularly important mechanistic link to Parkinson biology is provided by the report that Parkin, through its Caenorhabditis elegans homolog Parkinson disease related one, negatively regulates engulfment by promoting degradation of the Rac family small guanosine triphosphatase signaling component required for cytoskeletal rearrangement during corpse uptake; this finding connects Parkin directly to the cellular machinery governing phagocytosis and suggests that altered Parkin function could influence phagocyte behavior as well as neuronal vulnerability (PubMed:24625979). Finally, recent work showing that microglial mitochondrial state strongly correlates with expression of phagocytosis-relevant genes is also pertinent, because mitochondrial dysfunction is a central feature of Parkinson disease and may therefore secondarily reshape microglial phagocytic competence (PubMed:41388021). Taken together, the available evidence supports a model in which phagocytosis may represent a central interface between proteinopathy, glial immunity, myelin turnover, and Parkin-associated cytoskeletal regulation in Parkinson disease; depending on receptor usage and disease context, this pathway may either restrain pathology by clearing alpha-synuclein and debris or contribute to progression through maladaptive engulfment and glial-driven tissue remodeling.[PubMed:37671615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37671615) [PubMed:30944478](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30944478) [PubMed:40826098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40826098) [PubMed:33608912](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33608912) [PubMed:32582172](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32582172) [PubMed:24625979](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24625979) [PubMed:41388021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41388021) 

Building on this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment analysis provides an additional pathway-level context for considering phagocytosis in Parkinson disease. There were Parkinson disease-associated proteins analyzed in the function enrichment analysis for the pathway phagocytosis; however, the exact protein count was not provided in the available data. This pathway represents a multistep vesicle-mediated process in which extracellular particulate material is recognized, engulfed into membrane-bound phagosomes, and degraded after fusion with lysosomes, and its relevance to Parkinson disease is supported by the central contribution of microglia-driven clearance, astrocyte-associated phagocytic responses, removal of protein aggregates, damaged myelin, synaptic material, and apoptotic debris, as well as by the pathological consequences of both insufficient and excessive clearance. In the context of Parkinson disease, the enrichment of this pathway is biologically notable because even a single disturbance at any of the major sequential stages, including target recognition, cytoskeletal remodeling, phagosome formation, and phagolysosomal maturation, can shift the balance from tissue homeostasis toward chronic inflammatory stress and neurodegeneration. The pathway description further indicates that at least 3 major receptor classes participate in regulating these events, including scavenger receptors, purinergic receptors, and the TYRO3, AXL, and MER proto-oncogene, tyrosine kinase family, highlighting that phagocytic control depends on multiple parallel signaling systems rather than a single molecular entry point.

To connect this pathway-level interpretation with the molecular findings, the network view below illustrates how the identified proteins may relate to one another. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these proteins, together with the link to the STRING webpage.

With that broader network context in place, the following section introduces the significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
Among the proteins provided, CD209 stands out because it is directly involved in innate immune sensing of microbial glycans and in dendritic-cell-mediated pathogen recognition. Although CD209 is not a canonical Parkinson disease gene, its function may still be relevant to Parkinson disease through the increasingly recognized contribution of immune dysregulation, peripheral inflammation, and host–microbe interactions to neurodegeneration. Parkinson disease is associated with chronic activation of innate and adaptive immune pathways, and receptors such as CD209 may shape these responses by regulating how dendritic cells detect and process microbial products. This possibility is particularly noteworthy in the context of emerging evidence linking infections, gut dysbiosis, and systemic inflammatory signaling to Parkinson disease pathogenesis. By recognizing glycan-rich bacterial and parasitic antigens in a calcium-dependent manner, CD209 could influence antigen presentation, cytokine production, and downstream inflammatory cascades that may indirectly affect neuroinflammatory states relevant to dopaminergic neuron vulnerability. Its documented role in recognizing Mycobacterium tuberculosis further emphasizes its importance as a mediator of host–pathogen interactions, which may be mechanistically relevant to Parkinson disease insofar as persistent or exaggerated immune activation is increasingly viewed as a contributor to disease progression rather than merely a secondary consequence.[PubMed:16379498](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16379498) [PubMed:16092920](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16092920) [PubMed:21203928](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21203928)

### TYROBP causal network in microglia (WP:WP3945) 

The TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein causal network in microglia is an innate immune signaling pathway centered on TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein, a transmembrane adaptor that couples extracellular danger-sensing receptors on microglia to intracellular activation programs. This network is closely connected to triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2, integrin signaling, complement activation, phagocytosis, lysosomal trafficking, and the transition of microglia from a homeostatic state to a disease-associated inflammatory state. Across multiple neurodegenerative and injury contexts, activation of this pathway is accompanied by increased expression of genes such as TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein, triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2, complement C1q components, integrin subunit beta 2, Fc fragment of immunoglobulin E receptor Ig, and other microglia-enriched immune genes. Experimental studies in Alzheimer disease models indicate that loss of TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein suppresses disease-associated microglial programs, represses complement-related transcriptional changes, and improves electrophysiological and behavioral phenotypes even without reducing amyloid burden, supporting a causal role for this network in neuroimmune pathology rather than a merely reactive role. Additional work across aging, traumatic brain injury, epilepsy, and developmental microglia-like states further suggests that this pathway may function as a broad regulator of microglial activation, inflammatory communication, and phagocytic remodeling in the central nervous system.  

Against this biological background, the available literature supports an indirect but biologically credible link between the TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein causal network in microglia and Parkinson disease. Although the strongest direct mechanistic evidence for this pathway comes from Alzheimer disease and other neuroinflammatory conditions, several cited studies indicate that TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein sits within a conserved microglial immune module shared across aging and neurodegeneration, including Parkinson disease. In a cross-disease network analysis, TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein was identified as a human hub gene within a microglia-enriched module associated with aging, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and Huntington disease, suggesting that this pathway may mark a common neuroimmune response state relevant to Parkinson disease biology as well as to other degenerative disorders (PubMed:30733664). This observation is notable because aging is the major risk factor for Parkinson disease, and the same study argues that microglial gene regulatory programs are preserved across species and disease contexts. Further support comes from Parkinson disease proteogenomic work showing that leucine rich repeat kinase 2 variants regulate a set of proteins enriched in microglia and lysosomal trafficking pathways, including cluster of differentiation 68 and integrin subunit beta 2, with integrin subunit beta 2 identified as a causal protein candidate for Parkinson disease risk (PubMed:37422510). Because integrin subunit beta 2 is a canonical component of the TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein-associated microglial activation network, this finding places part of the pathway downstream of a major Parkinson disease genetic locus and links it to microglial lysosomal and trafficking dysfunction, processes already central to Parkinson disease pathogenesis. A review of imaging transcriptomics in neurodegenerative diseases further supports this interpretation by showing that regions vulnerable in Parkinson disease are enriched for immune, neuroinflammatory, and microglia-related gene expression programs, indicating that spatially patterned neurodegeneration is associated with innate immune activation rather than being purely neuron-autonomous (PubMed:33368775). At the same time, a commentary on substantia nigra single-nucleus data emphasizes that inherited Parkinson disease risk is more strongly associated with dopaminergic neurons and oligodendroglial lineage cells than with microglia, arguing against microglia as the primary cell type of genetic causation in Parkinson disease (PubMed:33206396). Taken together, the most balanced interpretation is that the TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein causal network in microglia is unlikely to represent the principal initiating pathway in Parkinson disease, but it may still act as an important modifier of disease progression by amplifying inflammatory signaling, complement activity, phagocytic remodeling, and lysosomal stress in response to neuronal injury and genetic perturbations such as leucine rich repeat kinase 2 dysregulation. Within this framework, the pathway is best viewed as a secondary but potentially therapeutically relevant neuroimmune program that may influence the tempo and severity of dopaminergic neurodegeneration in Parkinson disease.[PubMed:30733664](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30733664) [PubMed:37422510](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37422510) [PubMed:33368775](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33368775) [PubMed:33206396](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33206396) 

Building on this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment results provide a compact network-level view of how this pathway may intersect with Parkinson disease biology. There were 3 Parkinson disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein causal network in microglia, an innate immune signaling pathway that connects extracellular danger sensing to intracellular activation, phagocytosis, complement signaling, lysosomal trafficking, and the shift from homeostatic microglia toward a disease-associated inflammatory state. With a protein count of 3, this enrichment highlights a compact but biologically coherent signal centered on microglial immune regulation, which is highly relevant to Parkinson disease because neuroinflammation, complement-related activation, and maladaptive phagocytic remodeling are repeatedly implicated in disease progression and neuronal vulnerability. The figure below shows the protein-protein interaction network of these 3 enriched proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct inspection of the interaction evidence and network structure.

To further connect the network-level enrichment with individual molecular components, the function enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may help contextualize the observed signal. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
IL13RA1 is notable in the context of Parkinson’s disease because it participates in IL13 and IL4 cytokine signaling, pathways that are closely linked to immune regulation and neuroinflammation. Although IL13RA1 is not a canonical familial Parkinson’s disease gene, inflammatory signaling is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to dopaminergic neuron vulnerability and disease progression. IL4 and IL13 are generally associated with type 2 immune responses and can influence microglial activation states, thereby potentially modulating whether neuroinflammatory responses are neurotoxic or reparative. Through its partnership with IL4RA, IL13RA1 may therefore affect how glial cells respond to inflammatory cues in the substantia nigra, a brain region central to Parkinson’s pathology. This is particularly relevant because sustained innate immune activation, cytokine imbalance, and maladaptive glial responses have all been implicated in alpha-synuclein-associated neurodegeneration. Thus, IL13RA1 stands out less as a direct genetic driver of Parkinson’s disease and more as a plausible immunoregulatory node that could shape disease mechanisms related to chronic inflammation, neuronal stress, and progression of neurodegeneration.

### Integrin cell surface interactions (REAC:R-HSA-216083) 

Integrin cell surface interactions comprise a fundamental cell adhesion and signal transduction pathway through which integrin receptors on the plasma membrane bind extracellular matrix ligands and couple the extracellular environment to intracellular cytoskeletal and signaling networks. Integrins are heterodimeric receptors formed by alpha and beta subunits, and their activation is tightly regulated by conformational change, membrane lipid composition, and recruitment of cytoplasmic adaptors such as talin. A key mechanistic study showed that talin binding to acidic membrane phospholipids is required for integrin activation and focal adhesion formation, indicating that integrin signaling depends not only on receptor expression but also on membrane-associated activation machinery and linkage to the actin cytoskeleton (PubMed:30254158). Once activated, integrins organize focal adhesions and transmit bidirectional signals that regulate cell survival, migration, inflammatory activation, barrier properties, cytoskeletal remodeling, vesicular trafficking, and responses to mechanical stress. This pathway also intersects with phosphatidylinositol 3 kinase and protein kinase B signaling, platelet-derived growth factor receptor signaling, Wnt-beta-catenin signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune cell adhesion programs (PubMed:32509748, PubMed:39523497, PubMed:31699102, PubMed:36588107). In the central nervous system, integrin-mediated interactions are especially important at the neurovascular interface, where pericyte-derived vitronectin acting through integrin alpha five in endothelial cells helps maintain blood-central nervous system barrier integrity by suppressing transcytosis (PubMed:35294899). More broadly, extracellular matrix molecules and their receptors, including integrins, have been recognized as relevant therapeutic targets across central nervous system disorders including Parkinson disease, because they influence neuroinflammation, tissue remodeling, and cell-cell communication within the diseased brain (PubMed:25410365).

Against this mechanistic background, the available literature supports a biologically plausible connection between integrin cell surface interactions and Parkinson disease through three converging processes: neuroinflammation, blood-central nervous system barrier regulation, and extracellular matrix-dependent control of glial and immune behavior. Although the cited studies are not centered exclusively on Parkinson disease, they define mechanisms that appear highly relevant to disease pathogenesis. First, integrins are major regulators of leukocyte adhesion and trafficking in inflammatory conditions, and a central nervous system disease review explicitly identifies integrins and other extracellular matrix receptors as contributors to Parkinson disease-related pathology and as candidate therapeutic targets (PubMed:25410365). This interpretation is consistent with evidence that inflammatory cell recruitment into diseased nervous tissue depends on adhesion systems such as intercellular adhesion molecule one and leukocyte integrins, a process noted in a report discussing neuroinflammatory responses in Parkinson disease (PubMed:20641750). Second, neurovascular dysfunction is increasingly recognized in Parkinson disease, and integrin signaling has direct relevance because vitronectin-integrin alpha five signaling between pericytes and endothelial cells is required for blood-central nervous system barrier integrity (PubMed:35294899). Disruption of such adhesive signaling could therefore facilitate barrier leakage, inflammatory mediator entry, and amplification of microglial activation. Third, integrin pathways shape innate immune cell behavior in Parkinson disease models: a therapeutic nanoparticle study demonstrated that microglial targeting in Parkinson disease can be achieved through vascular cell adhesion molecule one and alpha four beta one integrin interactions, and modulation of these cells reduced oxidative stress, shifted microglia toward an anti-inflammatory state, and improved dopaminergic pathological features in mice (PubMed:33315369). Mechanistically, these disease-relevant effects are credible because integrin activation depends on talin-mediated membrane engagement and focal adhesion assembly (PubMed:30254158), while broader integrin signaling is known to control survival, migration, inflammatory signaling, and crosstalk with phosphatidylinositol 3 kinase and protein kinase B and other stress-response pathways (PubMed:32509748, PubMed:36588107). Taken together, the pathway may be related to Parkinson disease not as a single linear cause, but rather as a regulatory interface linking extracellular matrix alterations, vascular barrier stability, immune cell adhesion, and microglial inflammatory state, all of which could influence dopaminergic neuron vulnerability and disease progression.[PubMed:30254158](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30254158) [PubMed:32509748](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32509748) [PubMed:36588107](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36588107) [PubMed:35294899](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35294899) [PubMed:25410365](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25410365) [PubMed:20641750](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20641750) [PubMed:33315369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33315369) 

Building on this biological context, the enrichment result provides a more focused view of how this pathway may be represented within the Parkinson disease-associated protein set. There were 4 Parkinson disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of integrin cell surface interactions. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway connects extracellular matrix engagement to intracellular cytoskeletal and signaling regulation, and prior evidence has shown that talin-dependent membrane phospholipid binding is required for integrin activation and focal adhesion formation, thereby linking receptor activation state to downstream adhesive and mechanical responses (PubMed:30254158). In the context of Parkinson disease, this functional theme is relevant because integrin signaling influences several processes that are repeatedly implicated in neurodegeneration, including cell survival, inflammatory activation, barrier regulation, cytoskeletal remodeling, vesicular trafficking, and responses to mechanical stress, while also intersecting with phosphatidylinositol 3 kinase and protein kinase B signaling, platelet-derived growth factor receptor signaling, Wnt-beta-catenin signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune cell adhesion programs (PubMed:32509748, PubMed:39523497, PubMed:31699102, PubMed:36588107). The disease relevance is further strengthened by central nervous system evidence showing that pericyte-derived vitronectin signals through integrin alpha five in endothelial cells to maintain blood-central nervous system barrier integrity by suppressing transcytosis, a mechanism directly pertinent to vascular and inflammatory components of Parkinson disease pathobiology (PubMed:35294899). More broadly, extracellular matrix molecules and their receptors, including integrins, have been recognized as therapeutic targets across central nervous system disorders including Parkinson disease, supporting the interpretation that even a compact 4-protein enriched set may capture a biologically coherent and clinically meaningful adhesion-signaling module within the disease landscape (PubMed:25410365).

### protein complex involved in cell adhesion (GO:0098636) 

The pathway described as a protein complex involved in cell adhesion comprises multiprotein assemblies that physically and functionally connect cells either to the extracellular matrix or to neighboring cells. These complexes include integrin-associated focal adhesion structures, cadherin-catenin complexes, synaptic adhesion assemblies, and other receptor-scaffold systems that couple extracellular binding events to intracellular actin remodeling, membrane trafficking, mechanotransduction, and survival signaling. The cited literature illustrates the breadth of this pathway. Talin- and vinculin-associated adhesion machinery regulates filopodial capture and adhesive stabilization, demonstrating how structural adaptor complexes organize dynamic membrane protrusions and cytoskeletal anchoring (PubMed:30673614). In the nervous system, trans-cellular adhesion molecules such as activated leukocyte cell adhesion molecule, L1 cell adhesion molecule, close homolog of L1, semaphorin-associated receptor components, neurexins, latrophilin one, and contactin-associated protein-like two participate in axonal growth, guidance, synaptic specification, and maintenance of neuronal connectivity (PubMed:31300520; PubMed:22262843; PubMed:30028556). Additional studies indicate that adhesion complexes are not merely static structural units, but also signaling hubs linked to phosphatidylinositol three kinase and protein kinase B survival pathways, mammalian target of rapamycin complex two signaling, small guanosine triphosphatase activation, and calcium-permeable channel regulation, thereby integrating extracellular attachment with gene expression, cytoskeletal dynamics, and cell fate decisions (PubMed:31021484; PubMed:30156101; PubMed:28600358; PubMed:38631163). Taken together, this pathway may be viewed as a coordinated set of protein complexes that help maintain tissue architecture, enable neuronal wiring and synaptic communication, and regulate cellular responses to stress and inflammation.

Against this functional background, the potential relationship between this cell-adhesion-complex pathway and Parkinson disease can be considered through several convergent lines of evidence suggesting that neuronal adhesion systems are important for the development, maintenance, and stress resistance of dopaminergic circuits, while their dysregulation may accompany neurodegeneration. A particularly direct link is provided by work showing that activated leukocyte cell adhesion molecule promotes axonal growth of midbrain dopamine neurons through trans-heterophilic interactions with L1 cell adhesion molecule, close homolog of L1, and semaphorin receptor machinery; this observation is relevant because degeneration of midbrain dopamine neurons is the core pathological event in Parkinson disease, and impaired adhesion-dependent axon growth or maintenance could plausibly weaken nigrostriatal connectivity and limit repair capacity (PubMed:31300520). A broader mechanistic framework is suggested by the review of transient receptor potential melastatin seven, which identifies this calcium- and magnesium-permeable channel kinase as a regulator of migration, adhesion, axonal outgrowth, synaptic density, and neuronal survival, and further notes that altered expression or function has been associated with Parkinson disease, thereby linking adhesion-coupled signaling to both neurodevelopmental vulnerability and later degeneration (PubMed:38631163). Synaptic adhesion complexes are also pertinent, because neurexin-latrophilin trans-synaptic binding forms stable intercellular adhesion complexes, and contactin-associated protein-like two is a neuronal adhesion protein required for proper organization of excitable membrane domains and synaptic function; disruption of such adhesive architecture could contribute to synaptic failure that precedes neuronal death in Parkinson disease (PubMed:22262843; PubMed:30028556). In addition, transcriptomic analysis of substantia nigra pars compacta from sporadic Parkinson disease revealed upregulation of genes in cell adhesion and cytoskeletal categories together with inflammation-related changes, suggesting that adhesion remodeling may be part of the diseased tissue response, potentially reflecting reactive gliosis, extracellular matrix alteration, or compensatory restructuring of surviving neurons (PubMed:16179542). The relevance of adhesion complexes is further reinforced by studies showing that adhesion interfaces are tightly integrated with phosphatidylinositol three kinase and protein kinase B signaling and with mammalian target of rapamycin complex two-dependent control of adhesion molecules, pathways that have also been widely implicated in neuronal survival and degeneration (PubMed:31021484; PubMed:30156101). Collectively, these findings support a cautious interpretation in which protein complexes involved in cell adhesion may be related to Parkinson disease at multiple levels: they shape dopaminergic circuit formation, maintain axonal and synaptic integrity, couple extracellular cues to survival signaling, and undergo pathological remodeling in the degenerating substantia nigra.[PubMed:31300520](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31300520) [PubMed:38631163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38631163) [PubMed:22262843](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22262843) [PubMed:30028556](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30028556) [PubMed:16179542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16179542) [PubMed:31021484](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31021484) [PubMed:30156101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30156101) [PubMed:30673614](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30673614) [PubMed:28600358](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28600358) 

Building on this biological context, the enrichment result provides a more focused view of how this pathway may intersect with Parkinson disease-associated proteins.

There were 5 Parkinson disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as a protein complex involved in cell adhesion. This enrichment is biologically notable because the annotated pathway spans multiple adhesion-centered protein assemblies, including integrin-associated focal adhesion structures, cadherin-catenin complexes, synaptic adhesion assemblies, and receptor-scaffold systems that connect extracellular binding to intracellular actin remodeling, membrane trafficking, mechanotransduction, and survival signaling. In the context of Parkinson disease, an enrichment of 5 proteins within such a functionally integrated pathway is consistent with the importance of neuronal connectivity, synaptic maintenance, stress responsiveness, and inflammation-related signaling in disease biology. The cited evidence further indicates that these adhesion-associated complexes regulate filopodial capture and adhesive stabilization through talin- and vinculin-linked machinery, while neuronal adhesion systems involving activated leukocyte cell adhesion molecule, L1 cell adhesion molecule, close homolog of L1, semaphorin-associated receptor components, neurexins, latrophilin one, and contactin-associated protein-like two contribute to axonal growth, guidance, synaptic specification, and maintenance of neuronal connectivity (PubMed:30673614; PubMed:31300520; PubMed:22262843; PubMed:30028556). Additional studies show that these complexes also function as signaling hubs coupled to phosphatidylinositol three kinase and protein kinase B survival pathways, mammalian target of rapamycin complex two signaling, small guanosine triphosphatase activation, and calcium-permeable channel regulation, supporting a mechanistic framework in which 1 enriched adhesion-related module may influence several core cellular processes relevant to neurodegeneration, including cytoskeletal dynamics, gene expression control, and cell fate determination (PubMed:31021484; PubMed:30156101; PubMed:28600358; PubMed:38631163).
